Donald Trump Shooting Raises 'Lots of Questions'—Former FBI Official
Published
Jul 15, 2024 at 6:59 AM EDT
Updated
Jul 15, 2024 at 9:49 AM EDT
By
Sean O'Driscoll is a Newsweek Senior Crime and Courts Reporter based in Ireland. His focus is reporting on U.S. law. He has covered human rights and extremism extensively. Sean joined Newsweek in 2023 and previously worked for The Guardian, The New York Times, BBC, Vice and others from the Middle East. He specialized in human rights issues in the Arabian Gulf and conducted a three-month investigation into labor rights abuses for The New York Times. He was previously based in New York for 10 years. The Secret Service has many questions to answer after Saturday's attempted assassination of
Donald Trump
, a former senior
FBI
official said.
Frank Figliuzzi, former assistant director of FBI counterintelligence, told
Newsweek
that it hasn't yet been determined which agency was responsible for securing the rooftop overlooking the rally.
"The U.S. Secret Service used the phrase 'zero fail' to describe their mission. Saturday's incident was not a good day for the Service," he said.
Trump, the presumptive
Republican
nominee, was speaking at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on Saturday afternoon when a gunman fired multiple rounds from a roof overlooking the event.
Donald Trump pumps his fist as he is rushed offstage during a rally on July 13, 2024, in Butler, Pennsylvania. One person was killed in the shooting at a Trump rally.
Donald Trump pumps his fist as he is rushed offstage during a rally on July 13, 2024, in Butler, Pennsylvania. One person was killed in the shooting at a Trump rally.
Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
The former president was then seen grabbing his right ear with blood coming down his face before diving for cover. The Secret Service ran to protect him as he got to his feet.
The suspected gunman, 20-year-old Crooks of Bethel Park, Pennsylvania, was
shot and killed by the Secret Service
. In addition,
a rally attendee was killed
and two others were seriously injured.
Newsweek
sought email comment from the Secret Service and the Trump campaign on Monday.
Figliuzzi, who has over 20 years experience working in senior FBI roles, said that a thorough investigation is needed to determine what went wrong.
"The investigation into what failed will have to include how someone could get on a rooftop, with a rifle, within easy sniper range, without being stopped."
"If that rooftop was outside the hard perimeter, why? If that building was delegated to local or state police, why didn't they secure that building and rooftop? Lots of questions [and] no answers yet," he said.
Figliuzzi added that security will be tightened as the Republican National Convention begins, with heightened monitoring of potential threats.
"The lone actor or a small cell of independent actors is nearly impossible to thwart. Look for the FBI and the Secret Service to do 'knock and talks' with suspects to disrupt them from traveling," he said.
"The lone actor always has been the greatest challenge for counter-terror and law enforcement agencies. We live in a free society where law enforcement does not routinely monitor all communications or social media, or do we want them to.
"Yet, we can and must balance our civil liberties with maintaining security and safety. The bottom line is that when it comes to domestic American threats, unless a person or group is identified as planning violence, the police cannot just monitor their activities.
"In this shooting, there is no indication yet that the shooter was openly threatening the former president, nor even that he was known to law enforcement," he said.
